content: Angioedema is a condition characterized by swelling that occurs beneath the skin, unlike hives, which are surface-level swellings often referred to as welts. It is possible to experience angioedema without the presence of hives. The primary symptom of angioedema is the sudden onset of swelling beneath the skin. This swelling frequently occurs around the eyes and lips but can also affect the hands, feet, and throat. The swelling may appear as a localized area or spread more diffusely. In some cases, welts or surface swelling may also develop, which can be painful and itchy. These welts often turn pale and enlarge when irritated. The deeper swelling associated with angioedema can also cause significant discomfort. Additional symptoms may include abdominal cramping, difficulty breathing, swelling of the eyes and mouth, and chemosis (swelling of the lining of the eyes). Angioedema can result from an allergic reaction, during which histamine and other chemicals are released into the bloodstream. This release occurs when the immune system identifies a foreign substance, known as an allergen. However, in many cases, the exact cause of angioedema remains unknown.g., shellfish, nuts, eggs, milk), insect bites, medications (e.g., antibiotics like penicillin, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), and pollen. Angioedema and hives may also develop following infections or in association with other medical conditions, such as autoimmune diseases (e.g., lupus) or cancers like leukemia and lymphoma. A hereditary form of angioedema exists, which has distinct triggers, complications, and treatments, but this specific type is not covered in this discussion. If the throat is involved, a physical examination may reveal abnormal breathing sounds, such as stridor. In rare cases, blood tests or allergy testing may be performed to aid in diagnosis. It is crucial to seek medical attention if angioedema does not respond to treatment, becomes severe, or occurs for the first time. Emergency care is necessary if symptoms include abnormal breathing sounds, difficulty breathing, fainting, or wheezing. Treatment for angioedema depends on the severity of symptoms. Mild cases may not require intervention, while moderate to severe cases often necessitate treatment. Breathing difficulties represent a medical emergency. Pain relief can be achieved with cool compresses or soaks. Medications commonly used to manage angioedema include antihistamines, corticosteroids, epinephrine, ranitidine, and bronchodilators like terbutaline. In severe cases where breathing is compromised, a tube may need to be inserted into the throat to maintain an open airway. Patients diagnosed with angioedema should avoid certain medications, particularly ACE inhibitors such as benazepril, captopril, quinapril, ramipril, trandolapril, enalapril maleate, and lisinopril. It is essential to consult a healthcare provider before starting or discontinuing any medications. The prognosis for angioedema is generally favorable if it does not involve the airway. While the condition can be uncomfortable, it is typically harmless and resolves within a few days. However, complications such as an anaphylactic reaction or life-threatening airway obstruction can occur if the swelling affects the throat. To prevent recurrence, individuals should avoid irritating the affected areas and steer clear of known allergens. Medications should only be taken if prescribed by a healthcare professional.
